target: General SWE / backend software engineering internships (big tech + strong startups), 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
bullet_feedback.problem: Three mechanisms are unclear at once. 'strict access limits' could mean rate limits, query quotas, or permissions, and each one leads to a different design. 'the Claude skill' appears here before the next bullet explains what it is. 'category tree' doesn't say what the tree is keyed on or how a request is mapped to a node.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the most design-heavy bullet in the Capital One role (a constraint, then a precomputed index and a cache), but a reader can't rebuild the design from it. Interview question one will be 'what were the limits, and what does the tree index?', and the page gives no anchor for the answer.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what kind of access limit (rate, quota, or permission); what the category tree is keyed on; what the Redis key is and how cached workflows are invalidated when the table changes
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Swap the order of bullets 2 and 3 so the Claude workflow generator is introduced before it is searched. Then replace 'strict access limits' with the specific limit, and say what the tree is organized by before you name Redis.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting one large Claude skill into smaller sub-skills that call Python tools for search and validation, after CloudWatch and OpenSearch latency logs showed where time went
bullet_feedback.problem: The causal link is missing: the bullet doesn't say why splitting one skill into sub-skills made it faster (smaller prompts or contexts, running in parallel, or moving deterministic search and validation out of the LLM into Python). It also doesn't say what the logs showed.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: 'Split it into smaller pieces and it got faster' is the claim a senior engineer will push on. Without the reason, the 65% reads as prompt tinkering rather than profiling-driven engineering, even though the CloudWatch and OpenSearch detail suggests real diagnosis.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which step the latency logs pointed to, and which part of the split removed that cost
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Replace 'showed where time went' with the bottleneck the logs found, and tie the sub-skill split to that bottleneck. You can shorten the tool names to keep the bullet at two lines.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Rebuilt the legacy tool developers use to create test-data workflows as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation, and 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred it
bullet_feedback.problem: Five technologies (React, TypeScript, Electron, React Flow, Jest) carry the middle of the bullet, and none is tied to a decision. 'Jest-tested validation' doesn't say what is validated (workflow graph structure? field schemas?).
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: For a backend screen this reads as a frontend stack list. The engineering content, a validated workflow graph editor that replaces a legacy tool, is hidden behind the tool names.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with what the editor lets developers do and what validation catches. Keep Electron and React Flow only if they explain a choice; move React, TypeScript and Jest to Skills.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Automated retraining for a production Amazon Bedrock model that sorts research documents by importance: on an EventBridge schedule a larger LLM grades it, and it is fine-tuned only when those grades shift past a threshold
bullet_feedback.problem: The technical noun is blurred. 'sorts research documents by importance' hides whether this is a document classifier or a ranker. 'a larger LLM grades it' has an unclear referent: does it grade the model, its labels, or a sample of documents? 'grades shift' is a drift trigger that is never named as one.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is a good MLOps design (LLM-as-judge drift detection that gates fine-tuning), but the pronoun chain 'grades it ... it is fine-tuned' takes two reads. A hiring manager may not see that the candidate designed a retraining trigger.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: classifier vs ranker; what exactly the larger LLM grades (a sample of the model's outputs?); what 'shift' is measured against
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name the model as what it is (e.g. 'document importance classifier'), then say 'a larger LLM grades a sample of its outputs' and call the trigger what it is. Cut the second 'it'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Deployed a space-topic research tool for Amazon Leo's public-policy team and set it up for handoff with AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code and GitHub Actions CI/CD, so Leo engineers new to the project now maintain it on AWS Fargate
bullet_feedback.problem: 'space-topic research tool' doesn't say what the system does (search? scrape and summarize? a dashboard?). The bullet is mostly deployment tooling. Spelling out 'infrastructure-as-code' and 'CI/CD' after the tool names adds length but no information.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The handoff outcome is credible and good, but the reader can't connect this tool to the Kinesis and Bedrock bullets below it. The role reads as three separate systems instead of one pipeline.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the tool does for the policy team in one clause, and whether it is the same system the next two bullets describe
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Replace 'space-topic research tool' with a short description of what it does. Drop the parenthetical-style glosses (the Skills line already has them) to free up room.

bullet_feedback.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project targeting ICLR, built a Python pipeline that draws AnyGrasp candidates from multi-camera images as Open3D overlays and tuned prompts so a vision-language model picks the right grasp more often
bullet_feedback.problem: 'draws' is ambiguous: it can mean 'samples' or 'renders'. The real mechanism (render the grasp candidates as visual overlays so a VLM can choose among them) only comes through on a second read. 'more often' is the only result, and it has no scope.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the most novel idea on the page (visual prompting a VLM for grasp selection), and the ambiguous verb hides it. An interviewer asking 'how much more often?' gets no anchor from the page.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: 'renders' vs 'samples'; how grasp choice was judged against a reference (if a measured comparison exists)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Change 'draws' to 'renders' and structure the bullet as candidates, then overlay, then VLM choice. If no measured result exists, end on what the pipeline enables rather than 'more often'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Cut research-environment setup time 30% with uv dependency pinning and Docker, and added psutil time and memory profiling and Pytest unit tests to help the team find bottlenecks
bullet_feedback.problem: Four tool names (uv, Docker, psutil, Pytest) make up most of the bullet, and the second half ends on intent ('to help the team find bottlenecks') rather than a bottleneck that was found. Two unrelated tasks are joined with 'and'.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the weakest bullet on the page for a systems profile. It reads as tool hygiene, and it sits next to a far stronger research bullet.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the profiling surfaced a specific bottleneck
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Either cut the profiling clause to keep this a tight one-line reproducibility bullet, or name what the profiling found. Don't keep both halves at equal weight.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-founded a 110+ member student product studio that has shipped 5 live products, and personally built Redis caching in front of the Prisma ORM queries for one, Tortuga, a class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
bullet_feedback.problem: The clause 'for one, Tortuga, a class scheduler' is a stitched apposition that is hard to read aloud. The only number (20,000+ visits) measures the product's traffic, not the caching work, so the engineering claim has no result attached. The bullet also doesn't say what was cached or why.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A reader may credit the 20K visits to the cache, or think the cache is a name-drop. Either reading hurts in an interview ('what did the cache improve?'). Redis caching also shows up at Capital One without a result, so the pattern starts to look like a reflex.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what queries were cached and what problem that solved (load, latency, or DB connection limits)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Split the leadership claim from the engineering claim, or reorder to 'For Tortuga, a class scheduler that got 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, I ...'. Then name what the cache protected.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Building a RAG meal-suggestion feature for the official UMD app (GPT-4o mini, ChromaDB + SentenceBERT search); 93% of generated meals rated satisfactory by internal testers
bullet_feedback.problem: The tech parenthetical plus the semicolon chain is the telegraphic pattern this resume otherwise avoids. The bullet doesn't say what is retrieved (menu items? dining hall data?) or why RAG is needed instead of a plain query.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the only bullet that reads like a stack dump. It weakens the human-voice impression right before the strongest section on the page.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the retrieval searches over
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Rewrite as a sentence: what is retrieved, then how (SentenceBERT embeddings in ChromaDB), then the generation step. Drop GPT-4o mini to Skills if space is tight.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Compared B+ tree and LSM skip-list storage for the engine's event logs on identical 2M-record workloads: the B+ tree read 12.8x faster and answered range queries 22x faster, at the cost of 27% more disk
bullet_feedback.problem: The tradeoff shown is reads vs disk, but write throughput is the main reason to choose an LSM, and the bullet leaves it out. 'read 12.8x faster' doesn't say whether these are point lookups. The bullet also doesn't say whether both engines were implemented by the candidate.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Any storage-minded interviewer will ask 'and writes?' right away. Leaving writes out makes the comparison look either one-sided or set up so the B+ tree wins. If both structures are the candidate's own, that is a big signal and the page undersells it.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether both storage engines were built from scratch; the write-side result, if it was measured; point lookups vs scans
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: If both were built from scratch, say 'Implemented' instead of 'Compared'. Say 'point reads' if that's what was measured, and if write numbers were measured, state the tradeoff on both sides. Keep 'B+ tree' and 'LSM skip-list' exactly as written.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Sustained 1.26M events/sec end-to-end over the full replay, with price levels in a std::map of FIFO queues and a hash map from order ID to queue position for O(1) cancels
bullet_feedback.problem: 'hash map from order ID to queue position for O(1) cancels' will draw a pointed follow-up. A standard FIFO queue (std::queue or std::deque) can't erase from the middle in O(1). The claim holds only if the 'queue' is an intrusive or std::list structure and the map stores an iterator or node pointer. The throughput number also has no execution context (single thread? what hardware?).
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: As written, a strong interviewer could read this as a complexity mistake. The candidate will be fine if they can explain it, but the page invites a 'gotcha' moment on the best project.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: the queue's container type (linked list vs deque) and what the hash map stores (an iterator or pointer, not an index); single-threaded or not
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Replace 'FIFO queues' and 'queue position' with the actual container and handle (e.g. 'intrusive linked lists ... map from order ID to list node'). Optionally say 'single-threaded' if true.

page_feedback.problem: The strongest systems evidence on the page (order book and matching engine, B+ tree vs LSM, 1.26M events/sec) is at the very bottom. The Capital One and TerpLabs bullets in between lean toward AI and app features.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: On a skim the engineer type reads as 'cloud and LLM application developer' rather than the intended 'systems-oriented engineer'. The systems identity only shows up for readers who reach the Projects section.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the Experience order (brands carry the skim), but put the most systems-flavored bullet first within each role, e.g. Kinesis first under Amazon Leo and the precompute/cache bullet before the Electron rebuild at Capital One.

page_feedback.problem: Caching with Redis shows up twice (Capital One, TerpLabs) and neither instance says what it improved or how it was invalidated.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A repeated technique with no outcome starts to look like a name-drop. Cache invalidation is the obvious interview question, and the page doesn't set up an answer.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: In at least one instance, name what was cached and the problem it solved. Don't add metrics that don't exist.

page_feedback.problem: The Skills section has low-signal filler: 'data structures and algorithms', 'Jira', 'Agile'. C is listed but no bullet shows it.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: These items take up a line without adding credibility, and a listed language with no evidence invites a quiz question.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Cut the generic practice terms. Keep C only if you can back it up in an interview.

page_feedback.problem: Layout is clean, one page, consistent dates and headings. Body text is dense with little whitespace between roles, and italic titles and locations add visual noise.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Minor: it is readable at 100% zoom, but the page feels full.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: If space opens up from trimming tech lists, use it for slightly more spacing between roles rather than new content.

keep: Built a C++17 order book and matching engine and replayed 50.9M real IEX exchange messages through it without ever resyncing to the exchange's book, matching 99,122 of 99,123 fills and 100% of top-of-book prices
Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda

Writing Java logic that decides how much EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, setting upper and lower bounds that keep availability high without overspending, and backtesting the policies
Distinctive technical nouns to preserve verbatim: 'order book', 'matching engine', 'B+ tree', 'LSM skip-list', 'Kinesis streams', 'top-of-book'
